title: Perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:13–18)
hookLine: there is no fear in love
last: LOVE, AND DO WHAT YOU WILL.

cards: Watch a toddler at the playground. They run off, climb something too high, look around, and find their parent's face. If the face is there, they go a little farther.
If it isn't, panic. Psychologists call this a secure base: a child who's sure of being loved explores more, not less. Fear shrinks the world; love widens it.
The writer of First John never read a psychology textbook, but he says something very close, in one short verse about what love does to fear.

teach.b: First he repeats a great line and adds to it. In the King James Bible: "God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him." Dwelleth means to live in, to make your home in.

Love isn't only something God does; it's a place you can live. Then the verse: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love."
Perfect doesn't mean flawless; the Greek means complete, full-grown, mature. Casteth out is a strong verb, the word for throwing something out the door.

teach.h: LOVE THROWS FEAR OUT THE DOOR.
teach.b: Love doesn't negotiate with fear; it shows it out. And fear hath torment: the word can also mean punishment.
The fear he means is the dread of being punished, the fear of a child who expects to be hit.

teach.h: THERE IS NO FEAR IN LOVE.
teach.b: A fair question: doesn't the Bible also talk about the fear of the Lord? It does, often. Many Christian teachers distinguish two kinds of fear.
One is reverence, awe before something holy, like standing at the edge of the ocean. The other is dread, cringing before a punisher. The writer seems to mean the second.

Reverence can stay; dread is what love throws out. And the context is judgment day: he says we can have boldness even then. Not because we're flawless, but because, as he says, as he is, so are we in this world.

how: Many Christians memorize 1 John 4:18 and pray it in times of anxiety, and pastors often use it to distinguish reverent awe of God from dread of punishment.

o: a deep awe before something holy
the guilt you feel after a wrong

games.q: you love God, and you still feel dread at the thought of judgment. what does the letter say?
o: perfect love casts out fear, even of judgment.
you should try to feel more afraid.
games.why: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment." the writer says we may have boldness in the day of judgment.

practice: Name one fear that has been with you lately, being left, getting it wrong, getting sick, and ask it gently what it's afraid will happen to you.

Then picture beside it the face of someone who loves you, or, if you pray, the love of God, and let love stand in the same room with the fear without arguing. Notice which one takes up more space after a minute.

wordCard.voice: Torment. The dread that perfect, full-grown love throws out the door, First John says, so that people need not live in fear of punishment.
